speaker: Max Levchin
title: Max Levchin - Building Affirm, PayPal, and Why He Only Starts Network Businesses
question: In consumer credit, why does revolving debt structurally trap borrowers in ways fixed-term installment loans do not?
guest: The goal is to fight revolving debt. Revolving debt for consumers is a profoundly bad idea. Humans are just not very good at computing exponential functions and revolving on a progressively larger amount. If you're in debt for $5,000, pay off a little, spend a little, and it's back to $5,000, and then the interest compounds again, next thing you know your balance is $10,000 and you really can't quite figure out what happened. What happened is people are very bad at estimating exponential curves. As profitable as it is for the industry, it's an unhealthy way to lead your financial life. With a simple-interest installment loan, you see upfront that you borrowed $1,000, signed up for $50 of interest, and halfway done you owe $525—that number cannot change, and you know you have six or twelve months to go. Credit itself is good and access to credit is really important, but permanent debt is terrible. The goal is giving people who need and can afford credit excellent access without getting into debt they can't explain or work out of.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core difference is amortization. An installment loan has a fixed schedule: each payment is sized so the principal reaches zero by a set date, and you cannot re-borrow what you have repaid. Paying as agreed guarantees you exit the debt.

Revolving credit has no such endpoint, and several features work together to keep balances alive:

Minimum payments are calculated as a small percentage of the balance (often about 1–2% plus interest and fees), so they shrink as the balance shrinks. Paying the minimum mostly covers interest, stretching repayment over decades and multiplying total cost.

The credit line replenishes as you repay, so principal paid down can be immediately re-borrowed, and new purchases get mixed into old debt.

Interest rates are typically higher and variable, and compound on unpaid balances, often daily. Carrying any balance usually forfeits the grace period, so new purchases accrue interest immediately.

Finally, the low required payment anchors borrowers behaviorally: it signals an acceptable amount to pay, while lenders profit most from those who revolve indefinitely.

So installment debt is self-liquidating by design, while revolving debt is open-ended by design.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Fixed-term installment loans enforce an automatic exit: payments are structured around a set maturity date, ensuring each installment retires a growing share of principal until the balance reaches zero. Revolving debt lacks both a payoff horizon and a closed principal balance, creating several interlocking traps. First, minimum payment formulas—typically monthly interest plus just one percent of principal, or roughly two percent of the total balance—barely reduce the underlying debt and shrink in dollar terms as the balance falls, stretching repayment across decades. Behavioral research shows these low minimums also act as psychological anchors that pull borrowers away from making larger voluntary payments. Second, because repaid principal immediately becomes available to borrow again, cash-strapped households routinely re-spend freed-up credit to cover ongoing expenses, resetting the debt cycle. Finally, unsecured revolving lines carry substantially higher, variable interest rates that compound daily, alongside late fees and penalty APRs that capitalize into the balance. Together, open-ended re-borrowing, shrinking minimums, and compounding high-rate charges turn short-term credit into indefinite interest servicing rather than scheduled debt retirement.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Revolving debt has no built-in end date. An installment loan amortizes: each fixed payment covers interest plus a set share of principal, so the balance reaches zero on a known date. A credit card's minimum payment is usually about 1–3% of the balance or interest plus 1%. That is barely more than the interest, so paying only the minimum can stretch a few thousand dollars over decades and multiply the total cost.

Several features make this worse. Credit cards charge much higher rates than most installment loans, often over 20% APR, compounded daily. Because the credit line refills as you pay it down, the borrower faces the temptation to borrow again every month, while an installment loan pays out once. Lenders can also raise rates on new balances and apply penalty APRs, so the cost isn't fixed. On top of that, people tend to anchor on the low minimum payment and treat it as the "right" amount.

These features don't hurt everyone equally. Roughly half of cardholders pay in full each month and pay no interest. The trap catches those who carry a balance, who are often the borrowers with the least financial slack.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Revolving debt, such as credit cards, structurally traps borrowers because it lacks the built-in exit mechanism of a fixed-term installment loan. Installment loans enforce a rigid amortization schedule: fixed payments are calibrated to pay down both interest and principal so the balance reaches zero on a set date, and the credit line closes once repaid. Revolving accounts, by contrast, are open-ended and allow borrowers to continuously re-borrow against their credit limit, constantly resetting the principal. Their minimum payments are typically set as a small percentage of the balance—barely covering high, often variable interest that compounds daily—so the required payment shrinks as the balance falls, stretching repayment across decades. This low minimum also acts as a psychological anchor, nudging borrowers to pay far less than needed to escape debt. Combined with penalty rates and fees that capitalize into the balance, revolving credit is designed to sustain an ongoing, high-yield balance rather than retire it.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Revolving credit, such as a credit card, lets borrowers carry a balance indefinitely as long as they make the minimum payment. That minimum is often tied to the outstanding balance, so it can shrink as the balance falls. At a high interest rate, much of each minimum payment can go toward interest, leaving little to reduce the principal. Paying down the balance also frees up credit that the borrower can use again. If they rely on the card for everyday expenses, new charges can offset what they’ve paid down.

A fixed-term installment loan typically has a payment schedule designed to cover interest and repay the full principal by a set date. Paying down the loan doesn’t replenish funds the borrower can draw from. Both types of debt can be expensive, but with revolving credit, staying current can mean making payments for years without getting much closer to being debt-free.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Revolving debt has no built-in payoff date. Its minimum payment often falls as the balance falls, so a borrower who pays only the minimum puts fewer dollars toward the debt over time while interest keeps accruing. Repayments also free up credit to spend again. A borrower can therefore make every payment on time and still owe roughly the same amount years later.

A standard fixed-term installment loan builds repayment into the schedule. Each payment covers interest and pays down enough principal to retire the debt by a specified date, and repaid principal cannot be borrowed again under the same loan. A revolving borrower can pay off the balance by sticking to a sufficient fixed payment and avoiding new charges, but has to supply the discipline that an installment schedule provides automatically.
